In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the mammalian genome.
the evolutionary history and evolution of protein coding genes in mammals, with special emphasis on human, mouse and pig.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
rodents and artiodectyls are more closely related to each other than to primates.
rodents and primates have evolved in a similar manner, whereas the pig has evolved in a different way.
the human lineage has experienced the most rapid evolution in terms of both synonymous and non-synonymous substitution rate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the human and mouse genomes are more divergent than previously believed, whereas the divergence of the pig and the mouse lineages is similar to that of the human and mouse lineages.
the human lineage appears to be more prone to positive Darwinian selection than the other two mammalian lineages, whereas the pig lineage is evolving at a faster rate than the other two.

we can now use the pig as a model for comparative studies with humans and mice, as the rate of evolution is similar to that of the mouse, but the pig is more similar to the human lineage in terms of dN/dS ratios.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the pig genome is a valuable resource for studies of mammalian molecular evolution.
the rate of evolution of protein coding sequences is higher in the rodent lineage than in the primate lineage.
there are a large fraction of genes that are not annotated as functional genes and that these may have been lost recently or may be functional in other species.
